title: Scott:
length: about 85 s (about 75 s without the optional row)
headline: Four times through prison. Now he helps people find work. His answer to anyone who doubts recovery: “Look at me.”
story: Ask Scott what he would say to someone who does not believe they can recover. His answer: “Look at me.” He went through the prison system four times. An 84-day voucher at a house in Omaha was where his life turned. He kept a job, got a car, and MHA just promoted him to employment specialist.
Peer support works for him because nobody is above anybody. It must feel warm, proud and hopeful. His past is told in his own words, then the video moves on with him.
do: Open on frame 1 with “I'd say look at me.” Hook text on frame 1.
Keep his own words for his past. No extra text about it.
Use the Terrapin chalk B-roll only where it matches his words.
Name super: first name, new job title, MHA Nebraska.
Hold 1 second after “chance” before the end card.
dont: Never use 01:46–02:56. He asked for it to be off the record.
No dark music, no slow-motion “before” look.
Do not cut inside his “God finds a way” line (03:34). Leave it out whole.
Leave out 07:07–07:20 (he says he does not know how MHA works), WRAP (07:27–08:07) and the podcast story (09:18).

transcript:
Auto-transcript of 20260910_C4826.MP4 (Scott, Terrapin Station, Omaha, 10 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels removed: the transcript labels the interviewer as Scott.
[00:00] (Interviewer) I'm going to have you start by introducing yourself, your position at Mental Health Association of Nebraska.
[00:09] My name is Scott Marinovic.
[00:11] I'm currently a peer support specialist with the Mental Health Association of Nebraska, but I recently received a promotion to employment specialist here in the Omaha area.
[00:23] So I'm excited about that.
[00:25] (Interviewer) How did you first come across MHA?
[00:28] A friend of mine from the past had introduced me to the organization.
[00:34] I wasn't sure that I would be considered for employment, but I went ahead and filled out the application while I was working another full-time job.
[00:43] Once I interviewed for here and eventually heard back, I thought it was a wonderful opportunity and was kind of in line with my belief system and moral compass.
[00:51] So I took it on with excitement, even with doing overnight shifts, which I had never done before. So it worked out great.
[01:00] (Interviewer) What makes peer support different from traditional support?
[01:05] Peer support doesn't feel so institutional, and it's just like everyone's kind of coming from the same playing field.
[01:16] It's not like anybody's above anybody or no one person in the relationship has all the knowledge and all the answers.
[01:25] It's okay to say you don't know and it's okay to not be okay on either side of the friendship, I would call it.
[01:33] (Interviewer) Is there a moment or moments that you still think about or have stuck with you? ... Tell me about a moment here that you still think about.
[01:46–02:56] OFF THE RECORD. Scott asked for this story to stay off the record. Not transcribed here. Never use any of it.
[02:58] (Interviewer) What would you say to someone who doesn't believe that they can recover?
[03:02] I'd say look at me.
[03:04] I mean, I was pretty hard and deep off into the drug scene and, you know, thought I was going to be scarface or become rich or famous off of it and I had this storyline in my head I wanted to execute so bad but, you know, after kind of being forced into sobriety became willingness and like I actually wanted it and like so just being forced into giving it a chance, you know, against my will turned into that's what I want it to be because I see there's a better life, you know, and I hope that everyone has that chance and maybe not by force through the law and jail and everything but one way or another God finds a way of finding them to make a change because, you know, life can be a lot better than the type of situations that doing drugs and alcohol kind of forces you into and makes you look like the worst of a person you probably really are and just kind of, yeah, but I've been able to turn it around so far and I have to keep working at it, you know, and but it's rewarding and it's motivating and, you know, I think other people see it so.
[04:07] (Interviewer) What do people get wrong about this work?
[04:13] I'm not really sure what the perception is I guess I never heard of peer support before I started working here all I ever knew is like maybe people at a work release center or like assistant managers at a halfway house type thing they get rent for free and they're kind of the main person at the house in charge of who stays and who goes and who tells the landlord of the house or, you know, which person gets written up at a, you know, institutional setting like a work release so I never knew there was a such thing as peer support but
[04:44] a lot of people would think that maybe it's just a job that someone goes to just to get a paycheck but in reality, you know, the support you can offer someone through your life experience is valuable and I think it gives a lot of the participants who come through here hope
[05:02] and, you know, sometimes even, you know, there's jobs through this place which also has helped me with my sobriety and recovery is just having a job that I do like and I feel like I make a difference even if it's kind of in a subculture underworld way and nobody else knows about it that's okay, you know, because it's fulfilling to me in my spirit so there's a that aspect to it I guess that people might not understand or think about.
[05:29] (Interviewer) If someone watching has never heard of MHA, what should they know?
[05:35] They should know it has potential to be like super impactful in the community.
[05:42] I personally have experienced going through the prison system four times and there's like the work release like if you're lucky enough to get parole and have some time in the community before you would have to serve your whole sentence behind bars or in a prison, you get out on work release and in Lincoln is where most of the work release space is but the population in Omaha is actually far greater and so a lot of the people from Omaha are kind of forced into going to Lincoln work release just to have some semblance of freedom and start a life again but they're starting a life where they're probably going to have to pause, stop everything they're doing and then come to Omaha anyway but if MHA is able to grow the way I envision it I guess and open more houses there'll be more bed space for inmates who are recently incarcerated, men and women, to get out and start their life over again where their family is and where they want to be and also fall within the rules and the law and their conditions of parole and so this housing gives people a great opportunity to actually land on their feet and get their life going.
[06:49] I know I personally went through something very similar.
[06:52] My probation officer allowed me to get an 84 day voucher at a house here in Omaha and I made the most of the situation and that's really where my life took a turn for the better and you know I maintained employment, got a car, started a new job I actually like and things of that nature and just kind of kept the momentum rolling from there ... (07:10–07:20 not used.)
[07:23] (Interviewer) How has rap impacted your life?
[07:27] Rap has not impacted my life as much as I would like it to yet because I haven't done all the training and things like that.
[07:36] But I do try to keep it in mind and some of the principles because I think it's important that everybody really has a vision of wellness for themselves and that does look different in certain settings like whether it be if you're in community housing or at a work setting, otherwise in a family scenario there's different applications to it that I think are very valuable but I'm not as cognizant of it as I would like because I haven't done all the training with it.
[08:08] (Interviewer) And then we'll have you do some short sentences. So the first one is my name is blank and I'm a blank at MHA.
[08:17] (Joking, 08:17–08:34.)
[08:35] I'll stick with the goofy sellers thing but I don't know what my role at MHA is as far as like, you know, but I like to lift everyone's spirits and give everyone a sense of value like they matter and then just be as helpful as possible, you know, in whatever way I can be and use my time wisely, you know, since I've been given such an awesome and unique opportunity to do something I like.
[09:08] (Interviewer) Hope looks like...
[09:12] Hope looks like you can actually achieve some of the dreams and things that you put your mind to.
[09:18] Like there was a guy on a podcast, he worked for Apple, him and his wife, and he was talking about like basically anything you can conceive in your mind with the money that Apple has that can make it come to life, you know what I mean? And I feel like that's true even without the unlimited money.
[09:35] And I still have hopes and dreams of mine.
[09:37] I may or may not ever reach them but I feel like, you know, just working and chipping away a little bit each day, each week and month, you know, I can see tangible results and if I live long enough, I can possibly achieve it, you know, even if it's not on the grandiose level that I hope for.
[09:54] And I think everybody, that sparks me every day, even if I'm tired and had four or five hours of sleep and, you know, just knowing that I'm working towards something.
[10:04] I think everybody should have that, you know, if not, maybe they need a life coach or a peer support to help ignite that in them, you know, give them purpose.
[10:13] (Interviewer) And then last one is, peer support is powerful because...
[10:20] Sometimes you just need somebody to sit there and go through it with you, whether it's like filling out a job application or making a phone call to get your car repaired or just running by a relationship issue with somebody or just venting something that you don't want to overtake your day.
[10:38] So maybe you have somebody you trust to keep something secret and just between you and them and laugh about it instead of being angry all day and carrying that hate with you and your spirit when really it's just a thought or, you know, part of your ego that wants to think something and it might be hateful or not in value with your, you know, your spirit and soul.
[10:56] And so you have an opportunity to just separate that thought from what you actually believe and want, you know, like I love people at the core and I think we're all on this planet together working together towards something positive, not like, oh, I hate this man or woman because of this and then feed into that all day long and then be on the whole other side of the spectrum from where you want to be. So if that makes any sense.
[11:22] (Crew) Awesome. Anything else? / Not a thing. / Go you. Good job.
